new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one listed work (Grierson 1928), which I checked in full. For extra coverage I re-a full-text search for stress/accent the other files saved in the same directory (So-Hartmann 1988 scanned, Tha Tun Pru 1934 djvu text, the ISO 639-3 CR 2014-063 PDFs and HTML) for stress/accent/tone/register: the only hits are So-Hartmann 1988 p. 98 ('Tone and/or register was not marked consistently in most of the lists, so I have not attempted to discuss it') and her note that only the Daai list marks tones (two contrastive tones in Daai, not Chinpon). Nothing on Chinbon stress was missed.

sources.note: Nothing about Uppu prosody. The only 'tones' remark is a subject report about the Ekai RTT storyteller ('especially different in tones and vocabulary', p.9), i.e. about Ekai vs Daitu/Khamaw/Saingbaung, not Uppu. Uppu content is lexicostatistic: 'Except for one comparison at precisely 70%, the Uppu [cnb] varieties share less than 70% lexical similarity with the Saingbaung and Khamaw varieties along the Dalet Stream. Thus, Uppu [cnb] should be considered a separate language from Saingbaung and Khamaw.' (p.16) and 'the Ekai, Saingbaung, and Khamaw do not understand Uppu [cnb]. The Daitu reported…

sources.citation: Language and Social Development Organization (LSDO). 2019. A Chin dialect survey (Part 2 of 2) [Data set], file 'Chin wordlist helps-with Uppu.xlsx': 462-item IPA wordlists (2005-2016, Paing Nan et al.) incl. Uppu [cnb] from Buddhagarma (Paletwa), Khaingzi (Minbya), Chin Letmon and Kyin Dwe (Kanpetlet), Yan, Natkyi, Cintwe, Saw, Khaici, plus Mayin (Ownwa), Lonpaw (Khoimalaung), Minkya (Chi). Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3345035 (also in Part 1, doi:10.5281/zenodo.3344667). CC-BY 4.0.
sources.note: No phonology content: segmental IPA transcriptions only (syllable dots, aspiration, voiceless sonorants, glottal stops); no tone digits, pitch diacritics or stress marks in any cnb column and no prose notes. This is the largest primary Uppu dataset located (12 lists) but it is wordlist-only data, not a statement.

sources.note: Typology field reads only 'SOV; negation is marked after the verb.' Dialects: 'None known. Lexical similarity: 50% with Asho Chin [csh].' Writing: 'Latin script, recently developed, has a small user community.' No mention of tone or stress. Later editions (25th 2022, 26th 2023 snapshots) are paywalled stubs; the visible headings add nothing.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2014. Change Request 2014-062: 'Request for New Language Code Element in ISO 639-3' for Minkya Chin [cmy], submitted by Abraham (Linguistic Society [Myanmar]); rejected 2015-01-12 (variety remains under Chinbon/Uppu Chin [cnb]). Dallas: SIL International. 3 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. The form gives names, location (20.59 N, 94.19 E), linguistic affiliation ('Minkya is also similar to the various Uppu lects [cnb] at 87-96% lexical similarity'), comprehension reports and language shift ('All but a few older Minkya people speak only Burmese today'); sections on literature/sources say 'same as on Request for Change form'. No phonology, no mention of tone, stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent the extracted text output for tone|tonal|stress|accent|phonolog: 0 hits).
